concepts.name: Temperature
concepts.statement: Temperature is operationally defined to be what we measure with a thermometer. Your senses of hot and cold are relative: tepid water feels cool to a hand that was in hot water and warm to a hand that was in cold water. Two accurate thermometers placed in the same water give the same reading. Many physical quantities are defined solely by how we measure them, and later in the chapter temperature gains a more physical meaning, tied to the kinetic energies of atoms and molecules.

concepts.name: Thermometer
concepts.statement: Any physical property that depends on temperature, and whose response to temperature is reproducible, can serve as the basis of a thermometer. Volume increases with temperature for most substances, which is the basis for the alcohol thermometer, the mercury thermometer and the bimetallic strip. Electrical resistance, color and the emission of infrared radiation serve as well. Because so many properties depend on temperature, the variety of thermometers is remarkable.

concepts.name: Temperature scales
concepts.statement: A temperature scale starts from two easily reproducible temperatures, commonly the freezing and boiling points of water at standard atmospheric pressure. The Celsius scale puts them at 0 °C and 100 °C and the Fahrenheit scale at 32 °F and 212 °F, so one Celsius degree is 1.8 times the size of one Fahrenheit degree. The Kelvin scale is the absolute scale of science. Its zero is absolute zero, its unit is the kelvin with no degree sign, and a kelvin equals a degree Celsius in size, so water freezes at 273.15 K and boils at 373.15 K.

concepts.name: Converting a temperature between scales
concepts.statement: Temperatures on the three common scales are converted with the equations of Table 13.1. Celsius to Fahrenheit multiplies by nine fifths and adds 32, Celsius to Kelvin adds 273.15, and the conversions between Fahrenheit and Kelvin, which look complicated, are simple combinations of those two. A temperature difference converts differently from a temperature: a change of one degree Celsius is a change of one kelvin and of nine fifths of a Fahrenheit degree, with no offset.

concepts.name: Absolute zero
concepts.statement: The concept of absolute zero arises from the behavior of gases. The pressure of a gas kept at constant volume falls in a straight line as its temperature falls, and the lines for different gases all extrapolate to zero pressure at the same temperature, −273.15 °C. This suggests that there is a lowest temperature, and other thermodynamic relationships lead to the same conclusion. At absolute zero, 0 K, molecular motion is at the minimum energy possible; most gases liquefy and then freeze before it is reached, and it is not actually possible to reach it.

concepts.name: Thermal equilibrium
concepts.statement: Two systems in thermal contact are in thermal equilibrium when they have the same temperature, so that no heat flows between them and neither temperature changes. Any two systems placed in thermal contact but isolated from the rest of the environment reach this state: heat flows from the hotter object to the cooler one until their temperatures are equal. That is why a thermometer, which actually takes its own temperature, reads the temperature of the object it touches once enough time has passed. A single object is in internal thermal equilibrium when no heat flows within it and its temperature is uniform.

concepts.name: Zeroth law of thermodynamics
concepts.statement: If two systems, A and B, are in thermal equilibrium with each other, and B is in thermal equilibrium with a third system, C, then A is also in thermal equilibrium with C. The conclusion may seem obvious, because all three have the same temperature, but it is basic to thermodynamics. It bears the name zeroth law because it comes logically before the first and second laws, although physicists stated it after them. It lets you trust two thermometers, each touching a different block on the same plate, to read the same number, and so it makes temperature a meaningful concept.

concepts.name: Celsius scale
concepts.statement: The Celsius scale is the temperature scale on which the freezing point of water is 0 °C and its boiling point is 100 °C, both at standard atmospheric pressure.

concepts.name: Degree Celsius
concepts.statement: The degree Celsius is the unit of the Celsius scale, one hundredth of the interval between the freezing and boiling points of water. It is the same size as the kelvin.

concepts.name: Fahrenheit scale
concepts.statement: The Fahrenheit scale is the temperature scale on which the freezing point of water is 32 °F and its boiling point is 212 °F, both at standard atmospheric pressure.

concepts.name: Degree Fahrenheit
concepts.statement: The degree Fahrenheit is the unit of the Fahrenheit scale, one hundred eightieth of the interval between the freezing and boiling points of water, so a degree Celsius is 1.8 times as large.

concepts.name: Kelvin scale
concepts.statement: The Kelvin scale is the absolute temperature scale of science. Its zero is absolute zero, and its unit, the kelvin, is written K with no degree sign and equals a degree Celsius in size, so water freezes at 273.15 K and boils at 373.15 K.

concepts.name: Thermal expansion
concepts.statement: Thermal expansion is the change in size or volume of a given mass with temperature. It is why hot air rises, since air that expands has a smaller density than the air around it and a larger buoyant force on a given mass, and it is why railroad tracks and bridges need expansion joints. Its cause is that an increase in temperature increases the kinetic energy of the atoms, whose small, rapid vibrations push their neighbors slightly farther apart on average, and that slightly greater spacing adds up to a larger body. For most substances there is no preferred direction, and the body grows by the same fraction in every dimension.

concepts.name: Linear thermal expansion
concepts.statement: The change in length of a body is proportional to its length and to the change in temperature, with a coefficient of linear expansion that depends on the material and varies slightly with temperature. Because a kelvin and a degree Celsius are the same size, the coefficient and the temperature change may use either. The equation is accurate for small changes in temperature and serves for large ones with an average value of the coefficient.

concepts.name: Thermal expansion in two dimensions
concepts.statement: Objects expand in all dimensions, so an area grows because both its length and its width grow. For small temperature changes the change in area is twice the coefficient of linear expansion times the area times the change in temperature, since each of two dimensions contributes the linear fraction.

concepts.name: Expansion of a hole
concepts.statement: If you cut a hole in a metal plate, the remaining material expands exactly as it would if the plug were still in place. The plug would get bigger, and so the hole must get bigger too: the ring of neighboring atoms on the wall of the hole push each other farther apart as the temperature rises, and the ring gets slightly larger. Holes do not close up when a body is heated.

concepts.name: Thermal expansion in three dimensions
concepts.statement: The change in volume is very nearly three times the linear coefficient times the volume times the temperature change. The equation usually uses a coefficient of volume expansion about three times the coefficient of linear expansion, as the values in Table 13.2 show almost exactly. Liquids and gases have only a volume coefficient, and the coefficient for gases is the largest of all and nearly the same for every gas.

concepts.name: Finding what spills from an expanding liquid
concepts.statement: When a full container and the liquid in it warm together, both expand, but the liquid expands more, and the amount that spills is the difference of their volume changes. Because the original volumes are equal, the three equations combine into one: the spill is the difference of the two volume coefficients times the volume times the temperature change. The same difference is why a gasoline gauge reads empty with less mass in the tank in summer than in winter, and why a beaker filled to the brim overflows as it warms.

concepts.name: Anomalous expansion of water
concepts.statement: Water is the most important exception to the rule that objects expand with increasing temperature. Above 4 °C it expands as its temperature rises, but between 4 °C and 0 °C it expands as its temperature falls, so that it is densest at 4 °C. The most striking effect is the freezing of a pond: water at the surface cools to 4 °C, sinks, and turns the pond over until the whole of it is at 4 °C; a surface layer that cools further is less dense than the water below and stays on top, so the surface freezes over and the ice insulates the water beneath, where fish survive the winter.

concepts.name: Thermal stress
concepts.statement: Thermal stress arises when something constrains thermal expansion or contraction. To find the pressure a heated body would exert if it could not expand, take the volume change it would make at fixed pressure and use the bulk modulus to find the pressure that squeezes that volume back out. Such pressures are typically enormous: gasoline held at fixed volume through a 20 °C rise would reach 1.83 × 10⁷ Pa, about 2500 lb/in², far more than a tank can hold. Thermal stress buckles rails, snaps power lines, cracks unevenly cooled glass, weathers rock and pavement, and bursts biological cells when food freezes.

concepts.name: Coefficient of linear expansion
concepts.statement: The coefficient of linear expansion is the change in length per unit length per degree of temperature change. It depends on the material and varies slightly with temperature, and its unit is the inverse degree Celsius, 1/°C.

concepts.name: Coefficient of volume expansion
concepts.statement: The coefficient of volume expansion is the change in volume per unit volume per degree of temperature change. For a solid it is very nearly three times the coefficient of linear expansion, and liquids have much larger values than solids.

concepts.name: An ideal gas
concepts.statement: Atoms and molecules in a gas are widely separated compared with their sizes, so the forces between them can be ignored except when they collide, and the gas expands to fill whatever volume it can reach. That is why gases have the largest coefficients of volume expansion and why they all have nearly the same one, when liquids and solids differ widely: the properties of a gas depend on how many molecules there are per unit volume and on temperature, not on what kind of molecule it is. A gas whose particles have negligible volume and interact only through perfectly elastic collisions is called an ideal gas, and room temperature air is one in most circumstances.

concepts.name: Ideal gas law
concepts.statement: The ideal gas law relates the absolute pressure of a gas, its volume, the number of atoms and molecules in it and its absolute temperature through the Boltzmann constant. It is an equation of state, a relation among the thermodynamic properties of a system. It first came from experiment: Charles' law says volume is proportional to temperature at fixed pressure, and Boyle's law says pressure times volume is constant at fixed temperature. It describes real gases under most conditions, and it holds for any gas or mixture of gases, since only the total number of molecules enters. Always use absolute pressure and absolute temperature.

concepts.name: Boltzmann constant
concepts.statement: The constant that turns the count of molecules and the absolute temperature into the product of pressure and volume is the Boltzmann constant, named for Ludwig Boltzmann, with the value 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K. Its unit says what it does: it relates an energy to a temperature, so that kT is an energy per molecule.

concepts.name: Using the ideal gas law as a ratio
concepts.statement: When a gas changes state with some of its properties fixed, write the law once for the initial state and once for the final state and divide one by the other. Whatever stays constant cancels, and so does the Boltzmann constant, leaving a relation among the quantities that changed. For a tire whose volume and contents do not change, the ratio of final to initial pressure equals the ratio of final to initial absolute temperature, which is why the temperatures must be in kelvins.

forms.condition: constant volume and number of molecules

concepts.name: Mole
concepts.statement: The mole is the SI unit for the amount of a substance, and it is convenient because the number of molecules in any ordinary object is enormous. One mole contains Avogadro's number of particles, whatever the substance, and a mole of any substance has a mass in grams equal to its molecular mass, which is read off the periodic table. The number of moles is the number of molecules divided by Avogadro's number.

concepts.name: Avogadro’s number
concepts.statement: Avogadro's number is the number of particles in one mole, 6.02 × 10²³ per mole to three significant figures. It honors Amedeo Avogadro, who proposed, correctly, that equal volumes of gas at the same pressure and temperature contain equal numbers of molecules. Since 2019 one mole is exactly 6.02214076 × 10²³ elementary entities. The number is so large that a mole of table tennis balls would cover the Earth to a depth of about 40 km.

concepts.name: Ideal gas law in moles
concepts.statement: Multiplying and dividing the ideal gas law by Avogadro's number turns the count of molecules into a number of moles and the Boltzmann constant into the universal gas constant. That constant is Avogadro's number times the Boltzmann constant: 8.31 J/(mol·K) in SI units, 1.99 cal/(mol·K) or 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) in others. Use the form of the law that matches what you know, the number of molecules or the number of moles, and the value of the gas constant that matches the units of the problem.

concepts.name: Molar volume at STP
concepts.statement: Standard temperature and pressure are 0 °C and atmospheric pressure. At STP the ideal gas law gives 2.68 × 10²⁵ molecules in every cubic meter of any gas, 44.5 mol per cubic meter, and 22.5 L per mole to the precision of three-figure inputs (the accepted value is 22.4 L/mol). Because the count is the same for every gas, the mass of a cubic meter follows from the molar mass alone. Dry air at 28.8 g/mol weighs 1.28 kg per cubic meter, so a living room holds about 90 kg of air, the mass of a person.

forms.condition: at standard temperature and pressure, 0 °C and 1 atm

concepts.name: Ideal gas law as energy
concepts.statement: Both sides of the ideal gas law have the dimensions of energy, joules in SI units. Pressure is force per unit area, so pressure times volume is force times displacement, which is work. The right-hand side is proportional to the translational kinetic energy of the molecules at that temperature, as the next section shows. A gas holds energy related to both its pressure and its volume, and the ideal gas law is another expression of the conservation of energy: the work of pumping up a tire goes into the pressure of the air and into warming the pump and the air.

concepts.name: Universal gas constant
concepts.statement: The universal gas constant is the product of Avogadro's number and the Boltzmann constant, R = 8.31 J/(mol·K). It plays the part for a mole of gas that the Boltzmann constant plays for a single molecule.

concepts.name: Kinetic theory
concepts.statement: Kinetic theory assumes that atoms and molecules are in continuous random motion, and it explains pressure and temperature from that assumption. When a molecule collides elastically with a rigid wall, the component of its momentum perpendicular to the wall is reversed, so the wall exerts a force on it and, by Newton's third law, it exerts a force on the wall. A huge number of molecules strike the wall in a short time, and we observe the average force per unit area. More molecules mean more collisions and more pressure; faster molecules mean harder collisions and more pressure.

concepts.name: Ideal gas law from molecules
concepts.statement: Following one molecule in a box gives the pressure of the gas. Its momentum changes by twice its perpendicular momentum at each collision, the average time between collisions with one wall is the time to cross the box and back, so the average force from one molecule is its mass times the square of its perpendicular speed over the length of the box. Multiplying by the number of molecules, replacing the perpendicular component by a third of the mean square speed because the motion is random and the three directions are alike, and dividing by the area of the wall gives the pressure. The result, PV = ⅓Nm v̄², is another expression of the ideal gas law, now in terms of the mass and speed of the molecules.

concepts.name: Thermal energy of a molecule
concepts.statement: Setting the molecular form of the ideal gas law equal to PV = NkT and rearranging shows that the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is three halves of the Boltzmann constant times the absolute temperature. This average kinetic energy is the thermal energy. The equation gives a molecular interpretation of temperature, valid for gases and reasonably accurate in liquids and solids. It defines temperature in terms of the energy of molecular motion, and at a given temperature it is the same for every kind of molecule.

concepts.name: rms speed
concepts.statement: Solving the thermal energy equation for speed gives the root-mean-square speed of the molecules, the square root of the average of the speed squared, which grows with the square root of the absolute temperature and falls with the square root of the mass of the molecule. It is surprisingly large, 511 m/s for nitrogen at room temperature, yet it produces no wind, because the molecules move in every direction alike and travel only a tiny mean free path between collisions. The speed of sound, about 340 m/s at room temperature, reflects it, which is why sound is faster in hot air and in light gases such as helium.

concepts.name: Finding the mass of a molecule
concepts.statement: The mass of a single atom or molecule is the molar mass, read from the periodic table in grams per mole and converted to kilograms, divided by the number of particles in a mole. A nitrogen molecule is two atoms of 14.0067 g/mol, so it has a mass of 4.65 × 10⁻²⁶ kg; a helium atom has 6.65 × 10⁻²⁷ kg. Every calculation of an rms speed or of a temperature from a speed passes through this step.

forms.latex: m = \frac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{number of atoms per mole}}

concepts.name: Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution
concepts.statement: The motion of any one molecule is random in magnitude and direction, but a gas of many molecules has a predictable distribution of speeds, the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, calculated from kinetic theory and confirmed by experiment. The distribution has a long tail, since a few molecules move at several times the rms speed, and its peak, the most probable speed, lies below the rms speed. As the temperature rises the whole distribution shifts to higher speeds and broadens, which is why a person with a fever loses more water from the linings of the mouth and lungs.

concepts.name: Escape of light gases from an atmosphere
concepts.statement: To escape Earth's gravity from the top of the atmosphere an object must travel at 11.1 km/s, and helium would need a temperature near 2 × 10⁴ K for its rms speed to reach that. Yet the air holds very little helium. The speed of an atom changes from instant to instant, and at any instant a small fraction in the tail of the distribution exceeds the escape velocity; over billions of years that fraction leaks away. Heavier molecules, oxygen, nitrogen and water, have smaller rms speeds, and so few of them ever reach escape speed that Earth keeps its atmosphere. The Moon's gravity is so much weaker that it has lost almost all of its atmosphere, and its daytime sky is black.

concepts.name: Condensation of a real gas
concepts.statement: Real gases behave like ideal gases at high temperatures, but at lower temperatures the interactions between molecules and the volumes of the molecules begin to matter. The molecules come very close, the gas condenses, and the volume drops precipitously as the substance becomes a liquid. Cooled further it becomes a solid, and the volume shrinks a little more but never reaches zero, because the molecules themselves have volume. High pressure can also liquefy a gas, which is how industry makes liquid carbon dioxide and liquid nitrogen.

concepts.name: PV diagram
concepts.statement: A graph of pressure against volume is a PV diagram. For an ideal gas at fixed temperature and number of molecules the product PV is constant, so each isotherm, a curve at one temperature, is a hyperbola, and the upper curves are the hotter ones. At lower temperatures the curves stop looking like hyperbolas, since the gas no longer behaves ideally and may contain liquid; along the flat part of a low isotherm the pressure stays constant while the volume changes, because the substance is changing phase.

forms.condition: ideal gas, constant temperature and number of molecules

concepts.name: Critical point
concepts.statement: Above a substance's critical temperature the liquid phase cannot exist at any pressure. The isotherm at that temperature is the highest one with a flat, two-phase part, and above it a gas compressed hard enough may reach the density of a liquid without condensing. The critical pressure is the minimum pressure needed for the liquid to exist at the critical temperature. Carbon dioxide cannot become a liquid above 31 °C, nor oxygen above −118 °C, so no amount of squeezing liquefies oxygen at room temperature.

concepts.name: Phase diagram
concepts.statement: A graph of pressure against temperature is a phase diagram: there are well-defined regions in which the substance is solid, liquid or gas, and the solid lines between them are the temperatures and pressures at which two phases coexist. For water the liquid-vapor curve gives the boiling point at each pressure, 100 °C at 1.00 atm rising to 374 °C at 218 atm, which is why a pressure cooker cooks faster; the solid-liquid curve gives the melting point, and for water it leans so that the melting temperature falls with increasing pressure, which is why a snowball packs and why tires melt snow into an ice layer. Knowing the pressure and temperature, you can read the phase off the diagram.

concepts.name: Sublimation
concepts.statement: At sufficiently low pressures there is no liquid phase, and the substance goes directly between solid and gas. The phase change from solid to gas is sublimation; it accounts for snow pack that is lost without ever running into a river, for the automatic defrosting of a freezer and for freeze-drying. For water there is no liquid below 0.00600 atm, while carbon dioxide sublimates at ordinary atmospheric pressure, which is why solid carbon dioxide is dry ice: it does not melt.

concepts.name: Triple point
concepts.statement: The three curves of a phase diagram meet at a single point, the triple point, where solid, liquid and gas all exist in equilibrium. For water it is at 273.16 K and 0.00600 atm, and because it is a single well-defined temperature and pressure it is a more accurate calibration temperature than the melting point at 1.00 atm, which is 273.15 K. Every substance has one, and Table 13.4 lists several.

concepts.name: Phase equilibrium
concepts.statement: Liquid and gas are in equilibrium at the boiling temperature. In a closed container the liquid boils and the gas condenses at the same rate, with no net change in their amounts, because molecules leave the liquid as gas as fast as gas molecules stick to the liquid. At a higher temperature the liquid boils faster, more molecules are in the gas, the gas pressure is higher and condensation speeds up to match, so the pair reaches equilibrium again at the new pressure. An open pot of water at 100 °C boils away, and an open glass at 20 °C evaporates, because the gas above them is air rather than pure water vapor. A gas below its boiling temperature is a vapor.

concepts.name: Vapor pressure
concepts.statement: Vapor pressure is the pressure at which a gas coexists with its solid or liquid phase. It is created by the faster molecules that break away from the liquid or solid and enter the gas, so it depends on the substance and on its temperature, and an increase in temperature increases it. Water evaporates and ice sublimates when their vapor pressure exceeds the partial pressure of water vapor in the surrounding gas, and droplets or frost form when it is less.

concepts.name: Dalton’s law of partial pressures
concepts.statement: The partial pressure of a gas is the pressure it would create if it alone occupied the total volume available, and in a mixture of gases the total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures of the components, assuming ideal gas behavior and no chemical reactions. This is Dalton's law, and it follows from kinetic theory: each gas creates its pressure by its own molecular collisions, independent of the other gases present, and pressures add as Pascal's principle says they do.

concepts.name: Vapor
concepts.statement: A vapor is a gas at a temperature below the boiling temperature of its substance, so that it can coexist with the liquid.

concepts.name: Partial pressure
concepts.statement: The partial pressure of a gas in a mixture is the pressure it would create if it alone occupied the total volume available.

concepts.name: Critical temperature
concepts.statement: The critical temperature of a substance is the temperature above which its liquid phase cannot exist, however great the pressure.

concepts.name: Critical pressure
concepts.statement: The critical pressure of a substance is the minimum pressure needed for its liquid phase to exist at the critical temperature.

concepts.name: Relative humidity and saturation
concepts.statement: Relative humidity tells how much water vapor is in the air compared with the maximum possible. At the maximum, saturation, the relative humidity is 100%, evaporation is inhibited and we feel hotter, because sweat no longer cools us. The amount of water vapor the air can carry depends on temperature through the vapor pressure of water: at 100% humidity the partial pressure of water vapor equals the vapor pressure, below it evaporation goes on, above it condensation. The water is not held by the air; the amount of water in air is set by the vapor pressure of water alone and has nothing to do with the properties of air.

concepts.name: Finding the saturation vapor density
concepts.statement: Water vapor behaves like an ideal gas. The density of vapor that creates a given partial pressure follows from PV = nRT, solved for the moles per cubic meter and converted to grams with the molar mass of water, 18.0 g/mol. At 20.0 °C the vapor pressure of 2.33 × 10³ Pa gives 17.2 g/m³, exactly the saturation vapor density in Table 13.5. The table's densities are the maximum amounts of water vapor a cubic meter can carry at each temperature.

concepts.name: Percent relative humidity
concepts.statement: Percent relative humidity is the ratio of the vapor density actually in the air to the saturation vapor density at that temperature, times 100. With Table 13.5 it answers many questions about a day's weather: air at 25.0 °C holding 9.40 g/m³ has a relative humidity of 40.9%, and the same air with a dew point of −10.0 °C has only 10.3%.

concepts.name: Dew point
concepts.statement: The dew point is the temperature at which the air's water vapor would be the saturation density, so that the relative humidity would be 100%. At that temperature water starts to condense out of the air as dew, fog or frost. The air temperature cannot fall below the dew point without water condensing, and condensation releases considerable heat, which holds the temperature up. That is why farmers watch the dew point, why desert nights are so cold and why fog forms as the evening cools.

concepts.name: Reading humidity from the saturation table
concepts.statement: Every humidity problem runs through Table 13.5. The vapor density in the air, the saturation density at the air temperature and the saturation density at the dew point are three entries of the same column. Any one of humidity, vapor density, dew point and temperature follows from the others. The humidity is the ratio of two densities, the dew point is the temperature whose saturation density equals the vapor density in the air, and the water that condenses when air cools is the difference of two saturation densities. Where a temperature falls between rows, interpolate.

concepts.name: Boiling point and pressure
concepts.statement: Water boils at 100 °C because that is where its vapor pressure reaches 1.01 × 10⁵ Pa, one atmosphere, so that it can evaporate without limit. Bubbles form because water holds dissolved air: a bubble at the bottom of a pot contains air and water vapor at a total pressure of 1.00 atm, and as the temperature rises the water vapor in it increases and the bubble expands to keep its pressure; at 100 °C vapor enters continuously, the bubble grows, its buoyant force grows, and it breaks away and rises. Where the pressure on the water is different the boiling temperature is different: higher in a pressure cooker or at depth, lower at altitude and in a vacuum chamber.

concepts.name: Evaporation cools what it leaves
concepts.statement: We keep cool in hot weather by evaporating sweat from our skin and water from our breathing passages, and high humidity inhibits that evaporation, which is why humid heat is worse. The molecules most likely to escape a liquid are those with the greatest speeds, so the molecules that remain have a lower average speed and a lower temperature; lowering the surrounding pressure lowers the partial pressure of water, speeds evaporation, and can cool food until it freezes, which is what a freeze-dryer does. Blowing hot air dries hair faster because the higher temperature raises the rate of evaporation.

concepts.name: Saturation
concepts.statement: Air is saturated when its relative humidity is 100%, so that it holds the most water vapor it can at its temperature and the partial pressure equals the vapor pressure of water.
